title: The Duckling Parade
sum: Ivy watches five ducklings hatch in Grandpa’s garden and follows their parade from the first swim to the big pond in the park, where the littlest one finally leads the way.

cast.d: a six-year-old girl who watches the duck family in Grandpa’s garden
cast.look: a six-year-old girl with curly brown hair in two puffs, a yellow raincoat and red rubber boots

cast.d: Ivy’s grandpa, who grows tomatoes and has a small round pond in his garden
cast.look: an older man with a gray beard, a straw hat, green overalls and a big black umbrella

cast.d: a mother mallard who nests under Grandpa’s lilac bush
cast.look: a brown speckled mallard duck with an orange-and-brown bill and a blue patch on each wing

cast.d: the smallest duckling, always last in line
cast.look: a tiny fuzzy yellow-and-brown mallard duckling with a dark stripe by its eye

cast.d: the biggest, yellowest duckling, always first behind Mama
cast.look: a plump bright-yellow mallard duckling with small brown patches

p: For four weeks, a mother duck sat on a nest under Grandpa’s lilac bush. Ivy called her Mama Duck. Every day Ivy peeked from the kitchen window. Every day Mama Duck sat very still.
Grandpa had one rule. “We can look, but we don’t go close,” he said. “A mama duck needs her space.” So Ivy looked, and looked, and looked.
One Tuesday morning, Ivy heard something new. Peep. Peep-peep. It was tiny and high, like a squeaky toy.
Ivy ran to get Grandpa, and they tiptoed out to the garden. They crouched behind the wheelbarrow to watch.
Mama Duck stood up and shook her feathers. Under her lay bits of eggshell, pale green and cracked. In the middle was a heap of fluff. Then the heap wiggled.
A head popped up. Then another, and another. Each duckling was yellow and brown, with a dark stripe by its eye. Some were still damp and spiky, like hair after a bath.
Ivy counted in a whisper. “One, two, three, four, five.” Five ducklings! The smallest one sat at the back, blinking at a ladybug.
“That little one needs a name,” said Grandpa. Ivy thought hard. “Tuck. He’s all tucked in at the back.”
Mama Duck kept her babies warm all day and all night. The next morning, she stepped out and gave one loud quack. Off she went, waddle, waddle, waddle.
The ducklings tumbled after her. First came the biggest one, so yellow that Ivy named her Sunny. Next came three ducklings in a wobbly bunch. Last of all came Tuck.
“Where are they going?” Ivy whispered. “To the pond,” said Grandpa. “Ducklings can swim when they’re one day old.”
The parade went along the fence, past the tomato plants. Pat-pat-pat went their little feet. Then Tuck stopped to stare at a snail.
Ivy counted the ducklings. Her finger stopped too soon. Somebody was missing! Then she spotted Tuck, beak to shell with the snail.
Mama Duck turned her head. “Quack!” It was short and sharp, like a whistle.
Tuck gave a peep and ran. He tripped over a root and rolled like a ball of yarn. Then he squeezed back in at the end.
Grandpa’s pond sat at the bottom of the garden. It was round, with lily pads and one grumpy frog. Mama Duck walked straight in. Plop!
The ducklings stopped at the edge. Sunny went first. Plop! Then the next one went, and the next, and the next. Plop, plop, plop!
Tuck stood alone on the bank. “Will he sink?” asked Ivy. “Look at his feet,” said Grandpa.
Tuck’s feet were gray and wide, with thin skin stretched between the toes. They looked like tiny flippers. Tuck jumped. Splash!
He went under and bobbed up like a cork. His feet pushed at the water, back and forth. Off he paddled after the others.
“One day you’ll be at the front,” Ivy told Tuck. But Tuck was busy paddling, at the very back of the parade.

art.s: Five fuzzy yellow-and-brown ducklings follow a brown mother duck in a line toward a small round garden pond, while a girl and her grandpa watch from behind a wheelbarrow.

q.q: Draw Tuck’s foot. Show the part that helps him swim.
look: a wide, flat foot like a flipper
q.e: What a flipper! That skin pushes lots of water.

q.q: Mama Duck was first in the parade. Who was last?
q.e: Mama Duck first, Sunny next, and little Tuck last of all.

q.q: Tuck stopped to look at a snail. How many ducklings were still in line?
q.e: Five ducklings, and one stopped for the snail. That left four in line.

p: Three days later, the ducklings knew the way to Grandpa’s pond by heart. Mama Duck led the parade. Little Tuck came last, like always.
Ivy wanted to see them up close. She crept to the edge of the pond, where the grass was slippery. Whoops! Her foot slid, and one sneaker went right into the water.
Squish, squish. Her sock was cold and heavy. Water squirted out of her shoe with every step. “Yuck!” Ivy sat on a rock and pulled off her wet shoe and sock.
Out on the pond, Mama Duck tipped upside down. Only her tail stuck up. She was hunting for weeds to eat.
Up she popped. The water on her back sat in little round beads. Plip, plip, plip. They rolled right off.
Ivy looked at her soggy sock. Then she looked at Mama Duck. “Grandpa, how come she doesn’t get soggy?”
Grandpa was pulling weeds nearby. He pointed with a dandelion. “Watch what she does next.”
Mama Duck climbed out onto the grass. She twisted her neck around and poked her beak near her tail. Then she rubbed her beak along her feathers. Rub, rub, rub, down her wing and across her chest.
“There’s a little spot of oil by her tail,” said Grandpa. “She spreads it on her feathers, so water can’t soak in.” Ivy’s eyes went wide. “Like a raincoat!”
The ducklings were watching too. Five fuzzy heads turned around. Sunny pecked at her own tail. Tuck twisted so far that he fell over, feet in the air.
Ivy laughed. Then she saw something in the grass by the rock. It was a small brown feather with a bit of blue on it. Mama Duck’s!
Ivy had an idea. She kicked off her other shoe and peeled off the sock. This one was still dry. Her bare toes wiggled in the grass.
She dipped her finger in the pond. Drip. One drop fell on the feather. Drip, drip. Two more.
The drops sat on top of the feather, round as beads. Ivy tipped it. They rolled right off, and the feather was still dry.
Then she dripped water on the dry sock. Drip. Drip, drip. No beads this time. The drops sank in and left dark, wet spots.
“The sock drinks it,” said Ivy. “The feather doesn’t.” Grandpa held up his muddy hands. “That’s why ducks don’t need towels.”
Ivy made up a rhyme on the spot. “Drip, drop, roll off the top!” Over on the grass, Mama Duck gave a loud quack. “See?” said Grandpa. “She agrees.”
Ivy walked back to the house barefoot. In one hand she held her shoes and socks. In the other was a feather, dry as toast. Back by the pond, Tuck was still trying to reach his tail.

art.s: A barefoot girl sits on a rock by a small garden pond, dripping water onto a brown duck feather, while a mother duck rubs her beak along her feathers nearby.

q.q: Draw the feather with Ivy’s water drops on it. How many drops fell on the feather?
q.e: One drop, then two more. Three round drops!

q.q: What did Mama Duck spread on her feathers?
q.e: The oil from near her tail keeps water from soaking in.

q.q: Finish Ivy’s rhyme: “Drip, drop, roll off the ___.”
q.e: Drop and top rhyme. They end with the same sound.

p: On Saturday it rained all morning. Drops drummed on the roof and ran down the windows. Ivy pressed her nose to the glass. Where were the ducks?
“Can we go out?” she asked. “If you dress for rain,” said Grandpa.
So Ivy put on her raincoat first. Next came her red boots. Last came her hat with the floppy brim.
They went out under Grandpa’s big black umbrella. Pitter-pat, pitter-pat, went the rain on top. Ivy’s boots went splosh in every puddle.
The ducks were not in the pond. Only the grumpy frog was there, looking pleased. Mama Duck and her babies were out on the lawn. Rain beaded up on Mama’s back and rolled right off.
Worms had wiggled up out of the wet ground, and the ducklings were busy. Sunny grabbed one and pulled. It stretched like a rubber band. Slurp!
Ivy poked her face out from under the umbrella. She caught a raindrop on her tongue. It tasted like nothing at all, only cold.
Then the ducklings found the puddles. A big one lay by the path, and a small one by the shed. Three ducklings splashed in the big puddle. Two splashed in the small one, and one of them was Tuck.
Ivy jumped into the big puddle too. Splosh! Muddy water flew everywhere. The three ducklings flapped their tiny wings and ran for the small puddle.
Now the small puddle was full of ducklings. They were squished in so tight that nobody could splash. Tuck was standing on somebody’s foot.
All at once, the rain came down harder. The ducklings stopped splashing. Their fluff was getting damp and flat, and Tuck gave a small, shivery peep.
Mama Duck walked under the lilac bush and sat down. She puffed out her feathers and lifted her wings a little. One by one, the ducklings squeezed underneath.
Ivy counted the heads poking out. One, two, three, four. Then Tuck pushed in at the side. Pop! Sunny shot out the other side.
Mama Duck shuffled and spread her wings wider. Sunny scooted back in. Now all the little heads poked out in a row.
“Why do they hide under there?” asked Ivy. “Mama is warm,” said Grandpa. “Her body heats them up, and her feathers keep the rain off. It’s like a tent with a heater inside.”
Ivy looked down at her wet sleeves and shivered. Grandpa pulled her in close under the umbrella. His coat was warm and smelled like tomato plants.
Two under the umbrella. Six under the bush. Pitter-pat, pitter-pat, went the rain.

art.s: On a rainy day, a girl in a yellow raincoat and red boots stands under a big black umbrella with her grandpa, watching fuzzy ducklings peek out from under their mother’s wings beneath a lilac bush.

q.q: Three ducklings ran to the small puddle. How many ducklings were in it then?
q.e: Two were there already. Two and three more make five.

q.q: What sound did the rain make on Grandpa’s umbrella?
q.e: Pitter-pat, pitter-pat. Can you say it like the rain?

q.q: Draw how the ducklings stayed warm in the rain.
q.e: So snug! Mama’s warm body heats them up.

p: Two weeks went by. The ducklings grew bigger and louder, and they ate everything they found. Every afternoon, after a swim, they napped in a heap under the lilac bush.
One afternoon, Ivy came out to count them, like she did every day. “One, two, three, four.” She counted again. Four.
Ivy’s tummy went tight, and her hands felt cold. “Grandpa! Tuck is gone!”
Grandpa put down his watering can. They looked under the lilac bush. They looked behind the wheelbarrow. They looked in the tall grass by the fence.
Something rustled in the grass. Ivy dove for it. It was only the grumpy frog. He gave her a look and hopped away.
Mama Duck was looking too. She marched in circles by the pond. Quack! Quack! Quack! Loud and fast.
“Let’s stand still and listen,” said Grandpa. “A lost duckling peeps and peeps.” Ivy shut her eyes tight.
She heard the wind in the leaves. She heard a bee buzz past her ear. She heard Mama Duck. And then, very small and far away, she heard a peep.
Ivy opened her eyes. “Over there! By the shed!” Grandpa cupped a hand behind his ear. “I hear it too.”
Next to the shed, Grandpa’s old flowerpots lay on their sides in a row. There were five of them. The first pot was big. Each one after it was a little smaller, and the last one was tiny.
Ivy peeked into the first pot. Only dirt. The next pot had a spider in it. The next one had an old tennis ball.
Peep! It was louder now. Ivy crouched down by the fourth pot and looked in.
There was Tuck, curled up in a fuzzy ball. The sun had warmed the pot like a mug of cocoa. Tuck had crawled in for a nap and woken up all alone. He blinked up at Ivy. “Peep?”
Ivy laughed so hard she sat down in the grass. “You silly duck! We looked everywhere!”
Tuck waddled out of the pot and shook his fluff. Then he heard Mama’s quack. Off he ran across the lawn, peep-peep-peep, as fast as his feet could go.
Mama Duck stopped quacking. She touched Tuck all over with her beak, from his head to his tail. Then she tucked him under her wing.
Ivy counted one more time. “One, two, three, four, five.” Her hands felt warm again. Grandpa let out a big breath, like a balloon going flat.
That evening, Ivy turned all five flowerpots upside down. Just in case.

art.s: A girl crouches beside a row of five flowerpots lying on their sides, from big to tiny, and finds a small duckling asleep in the fourth pot.

q.q: Ivy counted only four ducklings. How did she feel?
q.e: Her tummy went tight. That is what worried feels like.

q.q: Ivy shut her eyes. Which part of her body helped her find Tuck?
q.e: Ivy listened hard and heard Tuck’s tiny peep.

q.q: Draw Grandpa’s five flowerpots in a row, from biggest to smallest. Put Tuck in the fourth pot!
look: each pot a little smaller than the one before
q.e: Big, smaller, smallest, and Tuck snug in pot number four!

p: By the end of June, the ducklings were almost as big as Grandpa’s slippers. Small brown feathers were poking out through their yellow fluff. Tuck looked like he had put his coat on halfway.
Grandpa’s little pond was getting crowded. When all the ducks jumped in at once, water sloshed over the sides. The grumpy frog had moved out.
Every morning now, Mama Duck waddled to the garden gate. She stared out through the bars. “She wants the big pond,” said Grandpa. “The one in the park.”
Ivy knew that pond. It had tall reeds all around, and it was big enough for toy boats. But to get there, the ducks had to cross the street.
So Ivy made a sign. She found a piece of cardboard and a fat red marker. It would say DUCKS CROSSING, but CROSSING was a long word.
“Two S’s,” said Grandpa. “Right in the middle.” Ivy wrote it in big red letters. At the bottom, she drew a duck with orange feet.
The next morning, Mama Duck quacked at the gate. The ducklings lined up behind her. Sunny was first, and Tuck was last, like always.
Ivy opened the gate and held up her sign. Grandpa looked both ways, stepped into the street and held up his hand. Out came the parade. Waddle, waddle, pat-pat-pat.
A boy on a bike came zooming down the street. Then he saw the ducks. Ding-ding! He rang his bell and stopped.
A red car stopped behind him. Then came a mail truck. The mail carrier leaned out of her window and laughed. “Well, look at that!”
Mama Duck did not hurry. She crossed one step at a time. Her five ducklings followed in a line. Ivy walked beside them, holding her sign up high.
Halfway across, Tuck stopped. He was staring at a shiny bottle cap in the road. “Tuck, not now!” Ivy whispered.
Mama Duck turned her head and gave her short, sharp quack. Tuck ran and caught up. The boy on the bike clapped.
Through the park gate they went, past the benches and the swings. And there it was, the big pond, shining in the sun.
Mama Duck walked into the water. Plop! Then came the ducklings. Plop, plop, plop, plop, plop!
They swam out in a line, with Mama first and Tuck last. Then a toy sailboat came gliding across the water, straight at them.
Mama Duck stopped. Quack! She turned around, and every duckling turned around too, right where it was.
Ivy gasped. Now the line was the other way around. Tuck was at the front!
Tuck paddled hard, and the whole family followed. He led them into the reeds, where tiny bugs buzzed over the calm water. Snap! Tuck caught one.
Ivy lowered her sign. “Look, Grandpa,” she said. “Tuck’s the leader now.”
Out in the reeds, one small duckling paddled at the front of the parade. Mama Duck swam at the very back, keeping watch.

art.s: A mother duck leads five ducklings across a quiet street while a girl holds up a cardboard sign that says DUCKS CROSSING, and a boy on a bike, a red car and a mail truck wait.

q.q: Draw a sign for the duck parade. What words will you write on it?
q.e: Everyone will stop for that sign!

q.q: How many ducks crossed the street in all? Count Mama Duck too!
q.e: Five ducklings and one Mama make six ducks.

q.q: What was poking out through the ducklings’ yellow fluff?
q.e: As ducklings grow, real feathers come in.

fin.q: Tuck was always last. After the sailboat, where was he in the line?
fin.e: Everyone turned around, so last became first!

fin.q: What kept Mama Duck dry in the pond and in the rain?
fin.e: The oil on her feathers made the water roll right off.
